captions.text: It feels like the global financial system is literally
ending. There are real fears that ATMs might stop
dispensing cash by Friday.
I remember that panic.
And in the middle of this total despair, you
have to be the lone contrarian looking at a
spreadsheet whispering to yourself, "No, things can't
possibly be that bad." That is the ultimate crucible
of investing. What this means for you is
that true contrarianism is deeply
deeply uncomfortable. It is not a fun
detached intellectual exercise you do on a
It's physical. It is.
Being too far ahead of your time, taking a
position before the pendulum starts to swing back is
practically indistinguishable from being wrong.
Your friends think you're crazy.
Your clients think you're reckless.
But standing alone in that discomfort is the absolute
only path to asymmetrical The numbers
from that exact era are staggering and they prove
the point. In the fourth quarter of 2008,
when everyone on television was screaming that the world
was ending and cash was the only safe asset,
Oak Tree and a few other distressed debt specialists
were actually buying up the debt of fundamentally sound
companies for pennies on the dollar.
Backing up the truck.
Exactly. [snorts] And those distressed debt purchases yielded
returns of 50 to 100% over the next 18
months. Skepticism isn't just saying,
"Well, that's too good to be true during a
tech bubble." It's having the guts, the pure
analytical courage to look at a market in freef
fall and say, "That's too bad to be true
during a global panic." That is a brilliant way
to frame it. Skepticism applies to extreme pessimism
